title: Uncountably Many Inequivalent Maximally Entangled Measurements For Two Qutrits
authors: Elna Svegborn, Jef Pauwels, Nicolas Gisin, Alejandro Pozas-Kerstjens
abstract: ArXiv:2607.16396v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Every two-qubit measurement basis composed of maximally entangled eigenstates can be transformed into the Bell basis via local unitary operations. For higher dimensions, in contrast, there exist inequivalent bases composed of maximally entangled eigenstates. Here, we provide a single-parameter family of two-qutrit maximally entangled measurement bases, and demonstrate that none of the bases are equivalent to each other under local unitaries. These bases are constructed from the continuous family of symmetric informationally complete sets of states in dimension three. By studying the local unitary bases that generate the family of two-qutrit maximally entangled measurement bases, we construct the first examples of wild error bases in the smallest dimension where these can exist. Finally, we discuss how distinct measurements in the family lead to differences in performance in several scenarios relevant in quantum information.
tldr: This paper constructs a continuous family of inequivalent maximally entangled measurement bases for two qutrits, demonstrating uncountably many local-unitary inequivalent bases.
motivation: In two-qubit systems, all maximally entangled bases are equivalent under local unitaries, but for higher dimensions the structure is richer. The authors aim to explore and classify the inequivalent bases for two qutrits.
method: The authors use the continuous family of symmetric informationally complete (SIC) sets in dimension three to construct a single-parameter family of two-qutrit maximally entangled measurement bases. They analyze local unitary equivalence and construct wild error bases.
result: They show that none of the bases in the family are equivalent under local unitaries, providing the first examples of wild error bases in the smallest possible dimension. They also demonstrate differences in performance across quantum information tasks.
conclusion: There exist uncountably many inequivalent maximally entangled measurement bases for two qutrits, with implications for quantum information processing and the classification of entanglement structures.

title: Holographic Quantum Codes With Trapped Ions
authors: Alex Steiner, Gerard Angl\`es Munn\'e, Robert Freund, Ivan Pogorelov, Michael Meth, Robert J. Harris, Gavin Brennen, Thomas M. Stace, Thomas Monz, Rainer Blatt, Felix Huber, Martin Ringbauer
abstract: ArXiv:2607.16503v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Holography is a central concept at the intersection of gravity, condensed matter theory, and quantum information, linking the interior bulk of a system to its boundary. A model realizing key features of holographic systems is the holographic pentagon code by Pastawski et al. Here we experimentally implement instances of the holographic pentagon and heptagon codes with trapped ions and test their properties: For the pentagon code, we recover logical bulk qubits from their nearby boundary and test the Ryu-Takayanagi entanglement area law. For the heptagon code, we show that the transversal Hadamard gate native to the constituent Steane codes induces a single-qubit, correctable error in the holographic code. Our implementation paves the way towards the use of holographic quantum codes for quantum information processing.
tldr: Experimental implementation of holographic pentagon and heptagon codes with trapped ions, demonstrating bulk-boundary mapping and the Ryu-Takayanagi entanglement area law.
motivation: Holographic quantum codes realize key features of the AdS/CFT correspondence and provide a testbed for quantum error correction and entanglement properties.
method: Trapped-ion quantum processor implementing the holographic pentagon code (Pastawski et al.) and heptagon code, with logical qubits encoded in Steane codes and transversal gates.
result: Recovery of logical bulk qubits from boundary measurements, verification of the Ryu-Takayanagi area law, and demonstration of correctable errors from transversal Hadamard gates.
conclusion: Holographic quantum codes are experimentally feasible with trapped ions, paving the way for quantum information processing and further studies of holography.

title: Geometric Power Capacity Of Coherent Ergotropy In Quantum Batteries
authors: Dong-Ping Xuan, Zhi-Xi Wang, Shao-Ming Fei
abstract: ArXiv:2607.16645v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We explore coherent ergotropy extraction in quantum batteries from a resource-geometric point of view. For an initial state [MATH], we quantify the coherent extraction process by the coherent ergotropy [MATH] and the coherent extraction distance [MATH] between the active state [MATH] and the passive state [MATH]. This defines the geometric power capacity [MATH], which measures the coherent ergotropy released unit minimal unitary distance. We prove that, for any driving Hamiltonian satisfying [MATH], the actual coherent discharging power is bounded by [MATH], showing that [MATH] is a capacity under unit driving norm rather than the power of a particular protocol. General bounds on [MATH] are derived by combining relative entropy bounds on coherent ergotropy with geometric bounds on the coherent extraction distance. We also formulate coherence measure induced bounds and protocol-corrected capacities involving the effective speed of a given Hamiltonian. Qubit and qutrit examples demonstrate that [MATH] captures a resource-geometric feature of coherent discharging beyond coherent ergotropy or coherence measures alone.
tldr: This paper introduces a geometric power capacity for coherent ergotropy extraction in quantum batteries, bounding the discharging power under unitary driving.
motivation: To quantify the maximum rate at which coherent ergotropy can be extracted from a quantum battery, beyond the total ergotropy or coherence measures alone.
method: The authors define the geometric power capacity as the ratio of coherent ergotropy to the minimal unitary distance between active and passive states, and derive bounds using relative entropy and geometric inequalities.
result: They prove that the actual coherent discharging power is bounded by this capacity for any driving Hamiltonian with unit norm, and illustrate the concept with qubit and qutrit examples.
conclusion: The geometric power capacity captures a resource-geometric feature of coherent discharging that is not captured by ergotropy or coherence alone, providing a fundamental bound on power extraction.

title: Mean-State Entropy Hierarchies And Classical Communication Through Quantum Convolutions
authors: Chunhe Xiong, Sunho Kim, Qing-Hua Zhang, Shao-Ming Fei
abstract: ArXiv:2607.16653v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum convolution provides a discrete-variable analogue of classical convolution, with the mean state capturing the stabilizer structure preserved under repeated convolution. We establish a finite-step entropy hierarchy generated by compatible stabilizer dephasings. Along every compatible isotropic flag, the entropy increases toward the mean-state entropy ceiling, while the relative-entropy distance to the mean state decomposes exactly into successive coherence losses and a terminal classical nonuniformity. Optimizing over compatible subspaces yields an intrinsic entropy profile of the state. For quantum convolutional channels, Weyl covariance reduces the one-shot classical communication problem to minimal output entropy. A spectral-transfer argument shows that suitable stabilizer inputs reproduce stabilizer-measurement distributions of the environment as channel-output spectra. This gives a computable Holevo lower bound over all complete stabilizer measurements; its compatible restriction is characterized by the entropy hierarchy and refines the previous mean-state bound of Bu, Gu, and Jaffe. The bound is exact for stabilizer-diagonal environments, for which the Holevo capacity is strongly additive, and yields a single-letter formula for a nonstabilizer qutrit family. The same family also exhibits a coexistence region with simultaneously positive classical and quantum communication rates.
tldr: Establishes entropy hierarchies for quantum states under stabilizer dephasings and applies them to bound classical communication capacity of quantum convolutional channels.
motivation: To understand the structure of quantum states under repeated quantum convolution and to derive computable bounds on classical communication over quantum convolutional channels.
method: Introduces compatible isotropic flags and stabilizer dephasings to generate a finite-step entropy hierarchy; uses Weyl covariance to reduce one-shot classical communication to minimal output entropy.
result: Derives a computable Holevo lower bound that refines previous mean-state bounds, exact for stabilizer-diagonal environments, and yields a single-letter formula for a nonstabilizer qutrit family.
conclusion: The entropy hierarchy provides a refined tool for analyzing quantum convolutional channels, and the capacity bounds are tight for certain environments, revealing coexistence of classical and quantum communication.

title: Intelligence-Guided Adaptive Purification For DDoS-Resilient Quantum Networks: A Cuda-q Based Study
authors: Santanu Ganguly
abstract: ArXiv:2607.16276v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum-repeater networks require adaptive control policies that balance entanglement generation rate, end-to-end fidelity, purification overhead, and memory-induced latency. This tradeoff becomes more complex when the classical control plane is degraded by cyber anomalies or denial-of-service traffic. We develop a CUDA-Q/SeQUeNCe co-simulation workflow for studying adaptive entanglement purification in heterogeneous linear repeater chains. CUDA-Q noisy quantum kernels are used to estimate primitive entanglement purification and swapping behavior, while SeQUeNCe provides an event-layer model for stochastic link generation, waiting-time-dependent memory decay, purification failure, and end-to-end swapping. Under stationary conditions, we compare no purification, local threshold purification, mean-field predictive purification, fixed purification, and a resource-penalized risk-aware predictive policy. In an 8-node chain, the resource-penalized risk-aware controller increases above-target delivery probability relative to fixed purification while reducing latency and purification overhead. We then couple the quantum-network controller to anomaly scores derived from the CSE-CIC-IDS2018 benign-to-SSDP intrusion-detection trace. During the attack period, the attack-unaware controller maintains high raw delivery, but its above-target entanglement delivery falls to 0.098+/-0.007; the IDS-aware resource-adaptive controller switches to more purification-heavy masks and increases above-target delivery to 0.344+/-0.011, closely matching the oracle-aware value of approximately 0.335. These results demonstrate that cyber-state awareness can improve useful quantum-network outcomes by trading raw throughput for fidelity-qualified entanglement delivery.
tldr: This paper proposes an adaptive entanglement purification framework for quantum networks that is resilient to DDoS attacks, using CUDA-Q and SeQUeNCe co-simulation.
motivation: Quantum repeater networks require adaptive control to balance entanglement generation, fidelity, and latency, especially under cyber attacks that degrade the classical control plane.
method: The authors develop a CUDA-Q/SeQUeNCe co-simulation workflow to study adaptive purification policies in linear repeater chains, comparing no purification, local threshold, mean-field predictive, fixed, and resource-penalized risk-aware policies, and coupling the controller with anomaly scores from intrusion detection traces.
result: The resource-penalized risk-aware controller increases above-target delivery probability from 0.098 to 0.344 during an SSDP attack, closely matching the oracle-aware value of 0.335.
conclusion: Cyber-state awareness can significantly improve useful quantum-network outcomes by trading raw throughput for fidelity-qualified entanglement delivery.

title: The Quantum Correction To Gaussian Information Geometry Is The Killing Form Of The Symplectic Algebra
authors: Christian Kerskens
abstract: ArXiv:2607.16376v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On the admissible cone [MATH] of Gaussian covariance matrices, the classical Bures--Wasserstein transport metric, the Fisher--Rao information metric, and the quantum Bures metric are individually well understood, but their mutual relationship is obscured by the operator equations defining them. Working with the contravariant (dual) metrics, we show that the exact difference between the dual quantum Bures metric and the dual Fisher--Rao metric is independent of the covariance matrix: it is identically the trace form, proportional to the Killing form, of the symplectic algebra [MATH], pulled back through the isomorphism [MATH]. The signature of this form on the Cartan decomposition reproduces the anisotropic stiffening of the quantum metric at the pure-state boundary: it is negative on the compact subalgebra [MATH], which carries the divergence, and positive on the noncompact complement. Because the correction is quadratic in the momenta, a no-go lemma shows it cannot arise from minimal coupling to a principal connection. We realize it instead through a Schur complement of a pseudo-Riemannian metric on a phase bundle, whose base reduction is the quantum Bures metric and whose horizontal metric is the classical-limit Fisher--Rao metric. All identities are verified numerically to working precision.
tldr: The paper identifies the exact difference between quantum and classical information metrics as the Killing form of the symplectic algebra, independent of the covariance matrix.
motivation: To clarify the relationship between classical and quantum information geometry, specifically the Bures and Fisher-Rao metrics, which are defined by operator equations that obscure their mutual relationship.
method: Working with contravariant (dual) metrics, the authors show that the difference between the dual quantum Bures metric and the dual Fisher-Rao metric is identically the trace form proportional to the Killing form of the symplectic algebra, pulled back through an isomorphism. They realize this correction via a Schur complement of a pseudo-Riemannian metric on a phase bundle.
result: The correction is independent of the covariance matrix and its signature on the Cartan decomposition reproduces the anisotropic stiffening of the quantum metric at the pure-state boundary. A no-go lemma shows it cannot arise from minimal coupling to a principal connection.
conclusion: The work provides a clear geometric interpretation of the quantum correction to Gaussian information geometry, linking it to the symplectic algebra's Killing form, and offers numerical verification.

title: Quantum Dynamics Of A Levitated Ferromagnetic Gyroscope
authors: Derek F. Jackson Kimball
abstract: ArXiv:2607.16592v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a quantum model for the rotational dynamics of a freely floating levitated ferromagnetic gyroscope (LFG), emphasizing the interplay between intrinsic spin [MATH], mechanical angular momentum [MATH], and magnetic torque. The conserved total angular momentum projection along the [MATH]-directed magnetic field [MATH], [MATH], is quantized, leading in the small-libration-amplitude limit to discrete precessional states [MATH] (eigenstates of [MATH] with eigenvalues [MATH]) and librational harmonic oscillator states [MATH] ([MATH]). The discreteness of the energies and dynamical variables is governed by the quantum precession scale [MATH], where [MATH] is the moment of inertia of the LFG. We find that the phenomenon of LFG precession persists into high-field regimes where the magnitude of the rotational angular momentum associated with precession exceeds the total intrinsic spin. We analyze the complementary quantum limits of localized semiclassical LFG orientation wave packets and exact [MATH]-eigenstates [MATH], clarifying the relation between classical precession signals and the underlying quantized spin-rotor dynamics. We further show that radio-frequency fields can drive [MATH] and [MATH] transitions, enabling ladder spectroscopy, tilt-angle control, and sideband-like coupling between precession and libration. The coupled dynamics also exhibit branch-point magnetic resonances where precession and librational motion become strongly coupled. These results establish a framework for using LFGs not only as ultrasensitive torque and magnetic-field sensors, but also as controllable mesoscopic quantum systems. The techniques developed here may be applied to searches for exotic, beyond-the-standard model spin-dependent interactions, ultralight dark matter, and spin-gravity couplings.
tldr: A quantum model for a levitated ferromagnetic gyroscope is developed, revealing quantized precessional and librational states and enabling applications in sensing and fundamental physics.
motivation: To understand the quantum rotational dynamics of a levitated ferromagnetic gyroscope, which can serve as an ultrasensitive sensor and a controllable mesoscopic quantum system.
method: The paper develops a quantum model for the rotational dynamics, quantizing the total angular momentum projection and analyzing the interplay between intrinsic spin, mechanical angular momentum, and magnetic torque.
result: Discrete precessional and librational states are identified, and radio-frequency fields can drive transitions between them, enabling control and spectroscopy.
conclusion: The framework establishes LFGs as controllable mesoscopic quantum systems for sensing and searches for exotic physics.

title: On The Information Required For Feedback Control
authors: Matthew P. Leighton, Jose M. Betancourt, Thierry Emonet, Benjamin B. Machta, Michael C. Abbott
abstract: ArXiv:2607.16639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Biological systems across scales, along with many engineering problems, must control noisy systems with limited information. Here we study information-limited feedback control of stochastic systems to achieve target steady states, and derive a lower bound on the information rate from controlled system to controller. This framework allows us to obtain performance-information Pareto frontiers for wide-ranging control problems with limited information. For systems with state-independent passive dynamics, the bound is saturated by an explicit optimal control protocol which probabilistically time-reverses the passive dynamics. We showcase these results through applications to nonlinear particle localization, microbial navigation, and experimentally realized information engines.
tldr: Derives a lower bound on the information rate required for feedback control of stochastic systems to achieve target steady states, and provides an optimal protocol that saturates the bound.
motivation: Biological and engineered systems must control noisy processes with limited information; understanding the fundamental information requirements is crucial for designing efficient controllers.
method: Uses information-theoretic tools to derive a lower bound on the mutual information rate between the controlled system and controller, and constructs an explicit optimal control protocol based on probabilistic time-reversal of passive dynamics.
result: The bound is tight for systems with state-independent passive dynamics, and the optimal protocol achieves the Pareto frontier between performance and information rate. Applications to nonlinear particle localization, microbial navigation, and information engines are demonstrated.
conclusion: The framework provides a fundamental limit on information-limited feedback control and offers practical optimal strategies, bridging information theory and thermodynamics of control.

title: Revisiting The Stability Of The Ingleton Inequality: A Tropicalization-Free Approach
authors: Laszlo Csirmaz
abstract: ArXiv:2607.16773v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The classical Ingleton inequality is known to hold for entropic points under specific exact conditional independence constraints. Recently, Matveev and Romashchenko (2026) investigated the stability of these implications, quantifying the extent to which the Ingleton inequality can be violated when a group of conditional mutual information terms is small but non-zero. While their proofs relied fundamentally on the complex framework of tropical probability spaces, we revisit these stability results using a completely tropicalization-free approach. By developing an alternative framework, we significantly streamline the underlying concepts and proofs, derive explicit error terms, and improve some estimates. Furthermore, we resolve an open problem posed in prior work by exhibiting a new infinite family of entropy inequalities that establishes the stability of the sum of two Ingleton expressions.
tldr: This paper provides a simplified, tropicalization-free proof of the stability of the Ingleton inequality for entropic points, improving error bounds and resolving an open problem.
motivation: The Ingleton inequality is a fundamental constraint on entropic vectors, and understanding its stability under approximate conditional independence is important for information theory. Prior proofs relied on complex tropical probability frameworks, motivating a more accessible approach.
method: The authors develop an alternative framework that avoids tropicalization, using combinatorial and algebraic arguments to derive explicit error terms and new entropy inequalities.
result: They obtain tighter error bounds for the stability of the Ingleton inequality and discover an infinite family of entropy inequalities that stabilize the sum of two Ingleton expressions, solving an open problem.
conclusion: The work simplifies and improves the understanding of Ingleton inequality stability, offering a cleaner proof technique and new results that advance the theory of entropy inequalities.

title: Tight Sample Bounds For Renyi And Min-Entropy Estimation
authors: Piotr Krysta Arman Adibi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.16966v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Estimating entropy from samples is fundamental in information theory and property testing. Both are special cases of order-[MATH] R'{e}nyi entropy, [MATH]. We characterize the sample complexity of estimating min-entropy and R'{e}nyi entropy for [MATH] and integer [MATH]; our lower bounds also hold for noninteger [MATH]. We prove that min-entropy estimation to constant additive accuracy has sample complexity [MATH]. The upper bound uses the largest empirical frequency and concentration via dyadic grouping. The matching lower bound hides a slightly heavier symbol at a uniformly random location. Thus, min-entropy requires [MATH] more samples than Shannon entropy and corrects a previously stated [MATH] characterization. For every integer [MATH], we prove the matching fixed-accuracy bound [MATH]. Previous results gave [MATH] for fixed integer [MATH] and [MATH] for all integer [MATH]. Our upper bound analyzes an unbiased falling-factorial estimator based on [MATH]-way collisions, while a hidden-heavy-coordinate construction gives the matching lower bound and shows that the factor [MATH] is unavoidable. For every real [MATH], we prove the uniform lower bound [MATH]. Finally, since [MATH], min-entropy uniformly approximates [MATH] when [MATH] is a sufficiently large multiple of [MATH]. motivation: Estimating entropy from samples is fundamental in information theory and property testing, but the sample complexity for min-entropy and Rényi entropy was not fully characterized.
method: The authors use empirical frequency analysis, dyadic grouping, unbiased falling-factorial estimators based on k-way collisions, and hidden-heavy-coordinate constructions for lower bounds.

title: Dissipative Stabilization Of Floquet-Engineered Many-Body Order
authors: Shreyas Raman, Robin Schafer, Alicia J. Kollar, Anushya Chandran
abstract: ArXiv:2607.16391v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Floquet driving underlies Hamiltonian and gate engineering, and produces dynamical orders with no equilibrium counterpart. These phenomena are, however, transient in well-isolated systems. We show that statically coupled dissipative auxiliaries cool the system toward low-energy states of the Floquet-engineered Hamiltonian, stabilizing orders in the steady state. The excess energy density is controllably small at high drive frequency and weak coupling and is captured by rate theory based on Fermi's Golden Rule. We numerically confirm robust cooling in a Floquet-engineered transverse-field Ising chain in both phases, and demonstrate discrete time-crystalline order, with a period-doubled magnetization response, in the steady state of a long-range Ising chain. Our results provide a rare analytical handle on the steady states of driven dissipative systems.
tldr: This paper shows that coupling a Floquet-driven system to dissipative auxiliaries can stabilize many-body order in the steady state, providing an analytical handle on driven-dissipative systems.
motivation: Floquet-engineered orders are transient in isolated systems; the goal is to stabilize them using dissipation.
method: The authors couple the system to static dissipative auxiliaries and use Fermi's Golden Rule to analyze the cooling effect, with numerical simulations on a Floquet-engineered transverse-field Ising chain.
result: They demonstrate robust cooling and stabilization of discrete time-crystalline order in the steady state.
conclusion: Dissipative stabilization offers a controllable way to realize Floquet-engineered orders, with potential applications in quantum simulation and information processing.

title: Satlock: Handover-Coupled Scheduling For Weather-Resilient Quantum Key Distribution Over Leo Constellations
authors: Md Jafrin Hossain Mohammad Arif Hossain
abstract: ArXiv:2607.17076v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Routing quantum keys over low-earth-orbit (LEO) satellite constellations is harder than classical routing: satellite handovers couple consecutive scheduling decisions, stochastic cloud cover can silently zero a ground link, and finite-key effects eliminate short, low-elevation passes entirely. We present SATLOCK, a handover-aware Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) routing framework that combines (i) a composite channel model incorporating atmospheric loss, pointing jitter, Markov cloud cover, decoy-state estimation, and finite-key correction; (ii) an integer linear program (ILP) giving a provable handover-aware throughput upper bound; and (iii) a decentralized deep Q-network (DQN) baseline for weather-adaptive online routing. We evaluate two contention regimes on a Walker constellation serving intercontinental demands. In low contention (16 satellites, 6 demands), the ILP delivers 1,311 Mbit while the strongest heuristics reach 95--96\% of ILP. In high contention (8 satellites, 12 demands), where handovers become binding, heuristics drop to 89.5\% of ILP. The DQN agent reaches 91.8\% and 84.6\% of ILP in the two regimes; it learns effective per-demand weather policies but is limited in aggregate by the lack of cross-demand coordination.
tldr: A handover-aware QKD routing framework for LEO satellite constellations that combines ILP and DQN to optimize key generation under weather and handover constraints.
motivation: Routing quantum keys over LEO satellite constellations is challenging due to satellite handovers coupling scheduling decisions, stochastic cloud cover, and finite-key effects that eliminate short passes.
method: The paper develops a composite channel model, an ILP for provable throughput upper bound, and a decentralized DQN for online weather-adaptive routing.
result: In low contention, heuristics reach 95-96% of ILP throughput; in high contention, heuristics drop to 89.5% and DQN achieves 84.6% of ILP.
conclusion: SATLOCK demonstrates the importance of handover-awareness and weather-adaptivity for QKD routing, with DQN learning effective per-demand policies but lacking cross-demand coordination.

title: A Novel Hybrid Quantum Reservoir Computing (nHQRC) For Phase Transition Detection In Non-Equilibrium Dynamical Systems
authors: Prashant M. Yawalkar Manoj B. Bhatkar
abstract: ArXiv:2607.16281v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The analysis of highly non-linear stochastic data within non-equilibrium dynamical systems requires computational frameworks capable of detecting latent phase transitions before systemic structural breakdowns occur. Traditional Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) are frequently bottlenecked by vanishing gradients, the barren plateau problem, and prohibitive training overheads. In this paper, we propose a novel Hybrid Quantum Reservoir Computing (nHQRC) framework, which bypasses these limitations by employing a frozen, disordered Transverse-Field Ising Model (TFIM) to project time-dependent stochastic driving forces into an exponentially large Hilbert space. To resolve the physical phase multi-wrapping vulnerabilities present in baseline quantum reservoir models, we introduce a lookahead-free, pre-amplification manifold scaling technique. Multi-qubit configurations are genetically optimized to the "edge of chaos," while quantum state tracking is performed by extracting von Neumann entropy ([MATH]) and exact mixed-state Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) to act as leading entanglement witnesses. Utilizing these quantum triggers as boundary constraints, trajectory predictions are constructed via a generative Stochastic Schr\"odinger Bridge (SSB) readout. By subjecting the quantum reservoir to an 8-dimensional non-stationary stochastic driving field, the framework significantly improves systemic drift-to-diffusion efficiency ([MATH]) and actively arrests maximum trajectory decay (MTD) by over 13% compared to standard classical benchmarks. This establishes a robust, [MATH] temporal overhead blueprint for near-term quantum regime detection and macroscopic subsystem stabilization.
tldr: A hybrid quantum reservoir computing framework using a frozen TFIM and von Neumann entropy/QFI for phase transition detection in non-equilibrium systems.
motivation: Traditional VQAs suffer from barren plateaus and training overhead; a reservoir approach bypasses these issues for detecting latent phase transitions.
method: A disordered TFIM reservoir projects driving forces into Hilbert space; von Neumann entropy and QFI serve as entanglement witnesses; a stochastic Schrödinger bridge readout predicts trajectories.
result: The framework improves drift-to-diffusion efficiency and reduces maximum trajectory decay by over 13% compared to classical benchmarks.
conclusion: The nHQRC provides a robust, low-overhead blueprint for near-term quantum regime detection and subsystem stabilization.

title: Simulating Neural Network Criticality And Resource Dynamics With Rydberg Gases
authors: Patrick Mischke, Herwig Ott, Michael Fleischhauer, Thomas Niederpr\"um
abstract: ArXiv:2607.16368v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficient operation of neural networks has been linked to criticality in their underlying non-equilibrium excitation dynamics. However, obtaining experimental evidence of this conjecture remains challenging due to limited control and undersampling in biological systems. Here, we experimentally explore neural network criticality using an ultracold Rydberg gas as a highly controllable simulator. We highlight the similarity of the excitation spreading via Rydberg facilitation and the synaptic connection of spiking activity of neurons, giving rise to distinct absorbing and active phases. We systematically explore and resolve criticality criteria, including power-law scaling of excitation avalanches and the emergence of universal avalanche shape collapse. Crucially, we implement a controlled gain mechanism to compensate for atom loss, mimicking metabolic resource replenishment and stabilizing the system in a controlled non-equilibrium steady state. We find peak temporal correlations at the critical point and stochastic oscillations with dragon king avalanches in the active phase, consistent with predictions for systems orbiting criticality. Our work establishes facilitated Rydberg gases as a platform for investigating criticality, resource dynamics, and emergent oscillations in neural networks.
tldr: This paper uses an ultracold Rydberg gas as a simulator to experimentally explore criticality and resource dynamics in neural networks.
motivation: Obtaining experimental evidence of neural network criticality is challenging in biological systems; a controllable quantum simulator can provide insights.
method: The authors use a Rydberg gas with facilitation to mimic synaptic connections, implement a gain mechanism to compensate for atom loss, and analyze excitation avalanches and temporal correlations.
result: They observe power-law scaling of avalanches, universal shape collapse, peak temporal correlations at criticality, and dragon king avalanches in the active phase.
conclusion: Facilitated Rydberg gases are a viable platform for studying criticality, resource dynamics, and emergent oscillations in neural networks.

The authors also analyze the occurrence of dragon king avalanches by comparing the tail of the size distribution to a power-law fit.

title: The Norton Theorem For Quantum Circuits And Systems
authors: Rahul Sarpeshkar Anthony J. Cressman
abstract: ArXiv:2607.16385v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is well known that classical analog circuits and systems benefit from the powerful Thevenin and Norton theorems. These theorems enable rigorous and exact mathematical simplification and representation of the effect of the rest of a system on the part we want to focus on. We show that there are corresponding versions of a "Quantum Norton Theorem" that enable exact simplification and reduction for quantum circuits and systems, not just for one port, but also for multiport and even open quantum systems. We demonstrate the method on two level systems, chains, system environment partitions, Lindblad examples, and Grover search. The Grover examples show how the reduced network isolates the bright pole governing ideal search and exposes how diagonal disorder transfers spectral weight into dark poles that degrade performance. By partitioning finite dimensional Schrodinger dynamics into retained and eliminated sectors, we show that Gaussian elimination gives an exact reduced equation in which the eliminated subsystem appears as a dynamical self energy and a source term. In the circuit representation, these terms become the Norton admittance and Norton current source seen by the retained quantum port. The same Schur complement construction extends to multiport reductions, composite system environment partitions, density matrix dynamics, and Lindblad evolution in Liouville space.
tldr: This paper extends the classical Norton theorem to quantum circuits, providing an exact reduction method for multiport and open quantum systems.
motivation: Classical circuit theory benefits from Thevenin and Norton theorems for simplifying complex networks; analogous tools are needed for quantum circuits to enable rigorous analysis and design.
method: The authors use Gaussian elimination and Schur complement constructions to derive an exact reduced equation where eliminated subsystems appear as dynamical self-energies and source terms, analogous to Norton admittance and current source.
result: The method is demonstrated on two-level systems, chains, system-environment partitions, Lindblad examples, and Grover search, showing how it isolates the bright pole and exposes the effect of disorder on search performance.
conclusion: The Quantum Norton Theorem provides a powerful tool for simplifying quantum circuits and systems, with applications to quantum network analysis and open quantum systems.

title: Entanglement Entropy In Quantum Networks With Tunable Geometry
authors: Andrea Azzali, Sridevi Kuriyattil, Andrew J. Daley, Maril\`u Chiofalo
abstract: ArXiv:2607.16394v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum many-body Hamiltonians with two-body interactions can be represented by graphs, with sites as nodes and two-site couplings as edges. We investigate how the geometry of these graphs affects transport and entanglement growth. To do so, we study dynamics for quantum hopping on a random graph model with an effective range parameter. Tuning it, we interpolate between nearest-neighbor and all-to-all graphs, identifying a new localization regime that is robust in both single-particle and finite-density cases. This provides a model of Anderson localization induced by structural disorder, with implications for amorphous materials and tunable-range analog quantum simulators.
tldr: This paper studies entanglement entropy dynamics in quantum networks with tunable graph geometry, revealing a new structural Anderson localization regime.
motivation: Understanding how graph geometry affects entanglement growth and transport in quantum many-body systems is crucial for designing quantum simulators and networks.
method: The authors model quantum hopping on random graphs with a tunable range parameter, interpolating between nearest-neighbor and all-to-all connectivity, and analyze single-particle and finite-density dynamics.
result: They identify a robust localization regime induced by structural disorder, distinct from standard Anderson localization, which persists at finite density.
conclusion: The findings provide insights into amorphous materials and offer a framework for analog quantum simulators with tunable-range interactions.

title: Host-guest Crystal Engineering Tailors The Room Temperature Spin Dynamics In Molecular Quantum Devices
authors: Ziqiu Huang, Angus Cowley-Semple, Irena Nevjestic, Yifan Yu, Mark Oxborrow, Sam L. Bayliss, Sarah K. Mann, Max Attwood
abstract: ArXiv:2607.16466v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Molecular materials that enable coherent control over an electron's spin state at room temperature are promising candidates for quantum technologies, including quantum sensors and ultra-low noise microwave amplifiers, known as masers. Host-guest molecular crystals enable independent control of spin-active guests and their local environments to enhance molecular spin properties and so improve device performance. Using electron paramagnetic resonance and optically-detected magnetic resonance, we demonstrate the ability to tune triplet population, depopulation, and spin-lattice relaxation by modulating host-dependent lattice rigidity and vibrational coupling to significantly reduce the operating requirements for building useful masers. Importantly, the most rigid host, picene, reveals the ability to slow spin-lattice relaxation without lengthening triplet lifetime, though at the cost of strain-induced line width broadening and reduced triplet spin polarisation. We also find that deuteration reduces the triplet resonance line width and vibrationally-mediated triplet depopulation. Consequently, we find that perdeuterated pentacene in perdeuterated p-terphenyl is the most viable candidate for building a continuous wave maser. This work demonstrates host-guest engineering as an important and practical method for tuning the spin-dependent performance of room-temperature molecular quantum technologies.
tldr: This paper demonstrates host-guest crystal engineering to tune spin dynamics in molecular quantum devices at room temperature, focusing on maser applications.
motivation: Molecular materials with coherent spin control at room temperature are promising for quantum sensors and masers, but optimizing spin properties requires independent control of spin guests and their environment.
method: The authors use electron paramagnetic resonance and optically-detected magnetic resonance to study triplet population, depopulation, and spin-lattice relaxation in host-guest crystals with varying host rigidity and deuteration.
result: The most rigid host (picene) slows spin-lattice relaxation without lengthening triplet lifetime, while deuteration reduces line width and vibrationally-mediated depopulation; perdeuterated pentacene in perdeuterated p-terphenyl is identified as the best candidate for continuous wave masers.
conclusion: Host-guest engineering is a practical method to tune spin-dependent performance of room-temperature molecular quantum technologies, particularly for masers.

title: Hamiltonian Lift Of Bures--Wasserstein Covariance Dynamics With A Spectral Floor
authors: Christian Kerskens
abstract: ArXiv:2607.16380v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Covariance dynamics on the positive-definite cone are commonly described by gradient flows, which encode dissipative relaxation but obscure the underlying phase-space structure. We construct a finite-dimensional Hamiltonian lift of covariance dynamics on Sym[MATH] equipped with the Bures--Wasserstein metric. The natural mechanical Lagrangian yields canonical momentum [MATH], where [MATH] is the Lyapunov operator, and explicit Hamiltonian [MATH]. Adding Rayleigh dissipation recovers the Bures--Wasserstein gradient flow in the overdamped limit. For a spectral-floor and trace-control potential, the quadratic fluctuation Hamiltonian around the isotropic equilibrium separates trace and traceless modes; the baseline stiffness diverges as [MATH] as the equilibrium covariance approaches the floor. The construction identifies a conservative parent system for constrained Bures--Wasserstein covariance relaxation and fixes the local stiffness scale induced by the spectral floor.
tldr: Constructs a Hamiltonian lift of Bures-Wasserstein covariance dynamics with a spectral floor, linking gradient flows to conservative mechanics.
motivation: Covariance dynamics on the positive-definite cone are usually described by gradient flows that obscure phase-space structure; a Hamiltonian formulation reveals the underlying conservative dynamics.
method: Uses the Bures-Wasserstein metric to define a mechanical Lagrangian, derives canonical momentum via the Lyapunov operator, and adds Rayleigh dissipation to recover gradient flow in the overdamped limit.
result: The quadratic fluctuation Hamiltonian around isotropic equilibrium separates trace and traceless modes, with baseline stiffness diverging as the equilibrium covariance approaches the spectral floor.
conclusion: The construction identifies a conservative parent system for constrained Bures-Wasserstein covariance relaxation and fixes the local stiffness scale induced by the spectral floor.

title: Qr-spps: Quantum-Native Retail Supply Chain Risk Simulation Via Vqe, Adapt-vqe Counterfactual Policy Ranking, And Dos-qpe Boltzmann Tail Risk Quantification
authors: Sumit Tapas Chongder
abstract: ArXiv:2607.16275v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical supply chain risk models treat node failures as statistically independent events, systematically underestimating correlated cascade failures across multi-tier supplier networks. We present QR-SPPS (Quantum-Native Retail Shock Propagation and Policy Stress Simulator), a quantum-native framework for retail supply chain risk analysis implemented on the Qiskit ecosystem using OpenFermion-based Ising Hamiltonian encoding. A 40-node, four-tier supply network is mapped to a 40-qubit Hamiltonian with ZZ coupling terms representing correlated supplier dependencies. A hardware-efficient Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) computes the stress ground state, revealing entangled cascade failures that differ substantially from classical Monte Carlo predictions. We further introduce the application of ADAPT-VQE gradient screening for counterfactual policy evaluation, enabling real-time ranking of six crisis interventions without repeated variational optimization. Finally, Density-of-States Quantum Phase Estimation (DOS-QPE) reconstructs the eigenspectrum through Trotter evolution and estimates Boltzmann-weighted catastrophe probabilities as a function of market-volatility temperature, providing a quantum-native tail-risk metric compatible with Value-at-Risk analysis. The framework demonstrates scalable quantum algorithms for correlated supply chain stress propagation, policy optimization, and systemic risk quantification while highlighting the exponential computational barriers faced by classical simulation at industrial-scale problem sizes.
tldr: A quantum-native framework for retail supply chain risk simulation using VQE, ADAPT-VQE, and DOS-QPE on a 40-qubit Ising model.
motivation: Classical models underestimate correlated cascade failures in multi-tier supply networks; quantum algorithms may capture entanglement-like dependencies.
method: Maps a 40-node supply network to a 40-qubit Ising Hamiltonian, uses VQE for ground state, ADAPT-VQE for counterfactual policy ranking, and DOS-QPE for Boltzmann tail risk.
result: Demonstrates that VQE reveals entangled cascade failures differing from classical Monte Carlo, and ADAPT-VQE enables efficient policy ranking without re-optimization.
conclusion: The framework shows potential for scalable quantum-native risk analysis but is applied to a specific domain problem with limited novelty in quantum information theory.

title: 80 Channel Photon Pair Source From A Thin-Film Lithium Niobate Racetrack Microresonator
authors: Mihir Chaudhari, Ian Christen, Xinyi Ren, Chun-Ho Lee, Tushar Sanjay Karnik, Reshma Kopparapu, Clayton Cheung, Kai-Chi Chang, Mengjie Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.16575v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nanophotonic platforms have multiple properties and features desirable for producing correlated photon pairs. In these platforms, spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) and spontaneous four-wave-mixing (SFWM) have been used to achieve photon pair production. By placing the nonlinear region in a resonant cavity, the source obtains an enhanced nonlinear interaction and naturally filters out photons by frequency according to the cavity linewidth. Among various platforms, X-cut thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) stands out for its strong second-order optical nonlinearity ([MATH]) and access to a strong platform for modulating light. Although previously demonstrated, present sources are limited in their photon pair channel availability, limiting the potential of quantum applications in quantum information processing, communication, and sensing that can scale in robustness by having access to multiple photon pair channels. To this end, we demonstrate a photon pair source on X-cut TFLN with 80 measured photon pair channels spanning the C and L optical bands with a frequency spacing of 49.5 GHz between photons. We characterize the second-order correlation function and pair generation rate (PGR) of 80 channels, the highest number of channels demonstrated to date, and achieve a pair generation of 125.7 kHz / {\mu}W after accounting for the cavity's escape efficiency. We also demonstrate heralded single photon operation by calculating a heralded auto-correlation dip of 0.0544 [MATH] 0.0054 with 2.2 mW of on-chip pump power. These findings demonstrate the promise of X-cut TFLN as a strong platform for quantum optical applications.
tldr: Demonstrates an 80-channel photon pair source on thin-film lithium niobate microresonator for quantum networking applications.
motivation: Existing photon pair sources are limited in channel count, restricting scalability of quantum information processing, communication, and sensing.
method: Uses spontaneous parametric down-conversion in an X-cut thin-film lithium niobate racetrack microresonator to generate photon pairs across 80 channels with 49.5 GHz spacing.
result: Achieves 125.7 kHz/μW pair generation rate per channel and a heralded auto-correlation dip of 0.0544, demonstrating high-quality heralded single photons.
conclusion: The source's high channel count and performance make it promising for scalable quantum optical applications, particularly in quantum networks.

title: Geometric Quantum Discord In The Black Hole Quantum Atmosphere
authors: Xiaofen Huang Siwei Li
abstract: ArXiv:2607.16641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the geometric quantum discord of bipartite Werner states influenced by Hawking radiation in the quantum atmosphere of a Schwarzschild black hole. We find that the geometric quantum discord in the physically accessible region exhibits a nonmonotonic behavior: it first decreases and then increases as the normalized radial distance increases, while the discord in the physically inaccessible region shows the exact opposite trend. A pronounced extremum of geometric quantum discord occurs precisely at the position corresponding to the peak intensity of Hawking radiation. Furthermore, we find that the Hartle Hawking constant and the event horizon radius exert opposite effects on the strength of quantum correlation redistribution: a larger Hartle Hawking constant enhances the redistribution effect, whereas a larger event horizon radius suppresses it.
tldr: This paper studies geometric quantum discord of Werner states in the quantum atmosphere of a Schwarzschild black hole, finding nonmonotonic behavior and a correlation redistribution effect.
motivation: To understand how Hawking radiation affects quantum correlations in curved spacetime, specifically bipartite entanglement and discord.
method: Analytical calculation of geometric quantum discord for bipartite Werner states in the Schwarzschild black hole background, considering both physically accessible and inaccessible regions.
result: Geometric quantum discord in the accessible region first decreases then increases with radial distance, with an extremum at the Hawking radiation peak; the Hartle-Hawking constant and event horizon radius have opposite effects on correlation redistribution.
conclusion: Hawking radiation redistributes quantum correlations between accessible and inaccessible regions, and the effect depends on black hole parameters.

title: Graph State Generation Based On Quantum Photonic Devices, Enabling Measurement-Based Quantum Computing
authors: Masoud Hakimi Heris
abstract: ArXiv:2607.16667v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photonic cluster states are fundamental resource for measurement-based quantum computing (MBQC), which is a promising approach for scalable quantum computing. These highly entangled states enable computation with applying local measurements rather than gate operations, which makes them essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing. Generation of the photonic cluster states requires high-quality entanglement and stability, which can be done by making use of cavity quantum electrodynamics (cavity QED), which is embedding quantum dots (QDs) into photonic microcavities. This method enables controlled single-photon emission and the entanglement of them, helping with key challenges in generating photonic cluster states. Enhancing the generation of the photonic cluster state requires improvement in the quality factor (Q-factor) and therefore, cooperativity of cavity and QD systems. A high Q-factor helps with reduction in photon loss and decoherence, ensuring more stable and high-fidelity quantum states. It also enables better light-matter interactions, improving cluster state quality. Cooperativity, which is a measure for the light-matter coupling strength relative to dissipation, directly impacts photon emission efficiency. Optimization of these parameters improves entanglement generation, which is essential for producing high-quality photonic cluster states. Therefore, optimized cavities are essential for improving the generation of the photonic cluster states. Scalability is also an important parameter for the generation of the large-scale cluster states used in quantum computing. In this paper, after reviewing MBQC, cluster states, and the generation of the photonic cluster states, we investigate the deterministic generation of the photonic cluster state resource for the purpose of MBQC, and highlights the importance of the inverse design techniques for this goal.
tldr: This paper reviews measurement-based quantum computing and proposes using cavity QED with quantum dots to generate photonic cluster states, emphasizing inverse design for scalability.
motivation: Photonic cluster states are essential for measurement-based quantum computing, but generating high-quality, scalable entangled states remains challenging.
method: The paper reviews MBQC and cluster states, then discusses deterministic generation using cavity QED with quantum dots, focusing on optimizing Q-factor and cooperativity.
result: It highlights that high Q-factor and cooperativity improve entanglement quality and photon emission efficiency, and suggests inverse design for scalable cluster state generation.
conclusion: Optimized cavities and inverse design techniques are key to advancing photonic cluster state generation for practical MBQC.

title: Identity-Paired Progressive Depth Training: When Trainability Persists Beyond Expressibility
authors: Athanasios Hadjidimoulas, Tirthak Patel, Anastasios Kyrillidis
abstract: ArXiv:2607.16800v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) are a leading paradigm for near-term quantum computing, yet their training suffers from sensitivity to circuit depth, initialization, and landscape pathologies such as barren plateaus. We study (PDT) -- a layerwise curriculum that trains a shallow circuit before appending new layers -- and identify a fundamental obstacle: fixed entangling gates (CNOTs) in hardware-efficient ans\"atze cause , an energy spike when new layers are added. We propose (IP-PDT), which appends forward/inverse block pairs -- each consisting of a standard rotation[MATH]CNOT block followed by its reverse -- that compose to the identity at initialization. Because the adjacent CNOT rings cancel, the effective circuit retains only surrounded by . We prove a simple : under this construction the variational manifold expands exactly once (when post-entangler rotations are first introduced) and then ; all subsequent depth increases provide pure overparameterization of single-qubit unitaries. Despite this saturation, progressive addition of rotation parameters can continue to improve optimization outcomes -- a phenomenon we term . We formalize IP-PDT as a continuation method on nested manifolds, prove monotone energy guarantees under an acceptance rule, and connect energy error to ground-state fidelity through spectral-gap inequalities. A detailed resource analysis shows that IP-PDT achieves lower total gate cost than both baselines by eliminating most CNOT gates.

title: EML-AirComp: Layered Over-the-Air Computation From A Single Nomographic Gate
authors: Onur G\"unl\"u
abstract: ArXiv:2607.16360v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Over-the-air computation (AirComp) exploits multiple-access superposition to compute functions of distributed data without separately decoding all terminal messages. We study a reusable two-input AirComp gate for the exp-minus-log (EML) operation [MATH], [MATH]. Thus, all internal nodes of a prescribed real-admissible EML tree reuse one gate type, avoiding node-specific nonlinear gate designs. Given an explicit EML tree whose intermediate logarithm arguments remain positive on a given compact domain, we derive additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) and coherent flat fading implementations under peak-power constraints. We then characterize the number of gate evaluations, the dependency depth, evaluation latency, node-wise feasibility, deterministic error propagation, positivity preservation, and a high-probability AWGN error bound for the complete tree. A four-terminal two-hop example gives explicit positivity and end-to-end error conditions, and a digital interface propagates quantization and gate errors across the tree.
tldr: This paper proposes a reusable two-input AirComp gate for the exp-minus-log operation, enabling layered over-the-air computation with a single gate type.
motivation: Over-the-air computation (AirComp) traditionally requires node-specific nonlinear gate designs; the authors aim to simplify this by reusing one gate type for all internal nodes of an EML tree.
method: The authors design an EML gate based on the exp-minus-log operation, derive AWGN and coherent flat fading implementations under peak-power constraints, and analyze error propagation and positivity preservation.
result: They characterize gate evaluations, dependency depth, latency, feasibility, error bounds, and provide a four-terminal two-hop example with explicit conditions.
conclusion: The proposed EML-AirComp framework enables efficient layered computation with a single gate type, with manageable error propagation and positivity constraints.
